propositions: Every unit of an application can read every application databag in the relation, including its own application's databag.
correction: Any unit can read the remote application's databag, but only the leader unit can read (and write) its own application's databag; a non-leader gets a permission error.
note: readLocalApplicationSettings calls GetRelationApplicationSettingsWithLeader (domain/relation/service/relation.go:317, s.leaderEnsurer.WithLeader); ErrNotHeld maps to ErrPerm. Interface comment at apiserver/facades/agent/uniter/service.go:492 says 'Only the leader unit may read the settings of the application in the local side of the relation.'

propositions: ntp, telegraf, nrpe and canonical-livepatch are subordinate charms of the monitoring/logging/sysadmin kind.
note: These are external Charmhub charms. The code only uses nrpe as a subordinate in a test fixture (charm.Meta{Name: "nrpe", Subordinate: true}), and ntp appears only as an interface name in relation tests. telegraf and livepatch do not appear as subordinates. Fine as a realistic illustration.

propositions: `ubuntu@22.04/stable` is a valid base string (channel with track/risk).
note: ParseBaseFromString splits on '@' into OS and channel, and ParseChannelNormalize handles track[/risk]. The Base.Channel comment at core/base/base.go:22-23 gives these same examples: "22.04" or "22.04/stable".

propositions: Juju registers providers for environments that are not clouds in the IaaS sense (unmanaged machines, LXD, Kubernetes) and treats them as clouds.
note: internal/provider has unmanaged, lxd and kubernetes alongside ec2/gce/azure etc. environs/interface.go:35 says an EnvironProvider is 'for either a traditional cloud or a container substrate like k8s'. In 4.1 the 'manual' provider type is named 'unmanaged' (providerType = "unmanaged", alias "null"), so any page that lists 'manual' is outdated.

propositions: The other party is called an 'observer'.
The owner/consumer roles are independent of the provider/requirer roles in the relation used to grant access.
correction: A secret has an owner (an application, unit or model) and consumers, the entities granted access to read it; these roles are independent of the provider/requirer roles of the relation the grant is scoped to.
note: The code never uses 'observer'. It uses 'consumer' throughout (SecretConsumerMetadata, the secret_unit_consumer and secret_remote_unit_consumer tables in domain/secret/state/state.go:978,982). Owner kinds are application, unit and model (core/secrets/secret.go:202-204). The independence part holds, since no role check was found.

propositions: Juju uses 'substrate' as a more general term for a cloud.
note: 'substrate' appears in code comments: environs/interface.go:35 ('container substrate like k8s'), rpc/params/model.go:183 ('the substrate the model is deployed to'), caas/broker.go:154 ('the CAAS substrate'). It is informal comment vocabulary, not a type or API term.

propositions: The offering model names a consumer application with a synthetic name of the form 'remote-' plus 32 hex characters (a dashless UUID).
The shown token fits that format.
note: RemoteApplicationNameFromUUID returns "remote-" + uuid with dashes stripped. The validator (core/application/name.go:23-28) requires exactly 32 chars that decode as a UUID. The example has 32 hex chars with version nibble 4, so it is valid. The UUID is freshly generated for the synthetic app (domain/crossmodelrelation/service/remoteapplication.go:244-252), not the consumer's own app UUID.

propositions: Some config values (antecedent unknown from the claim alone) can only be set at bootstrap and are read-only afterwards.
note: The claim doesn't say which keys 'these config values' are. Mechanism: controller config keys not listed in AllowedUpdateConfigAttributes cannot be changed after the controller is created. If the antecedent is such a controller key, the claim holds. If it is a model-config key (e.g. egress-subnets), it would be wrong. Check the antecedent against that list.

propositions: Creating a relation creates the relation databags.
correction: Adding a relation creates the relation and one endpoint per application, which key the application databags. A unit's databag comes into being when the unit enters the relation's scope, and settings rows are stored only when data is written.
note: AddRelation (relation.go:80) inserts the relation, endpoints, status and egress but no settings. setRelationApplicationSettings returns early when settings are empty (relation.go:~3976). EnterScope inserts the relation_unit (relation.go:1837) and sets the unit settings (relation.go:1845). Conceptually right, but the creation is lazy and partly per unit.

propositions: Juju adds an implicit `juju-info` provider endpoint to every charm.
That endpoint is meant to be consumed by a subordinate requiring interface juju-info with container scope.
correction: Every charm gets an implicit global-scoped `juju-info` provider endpoint; any charm with a `requires` endpoint of interface `juju-info` can consume it, and a subordinate typically does so with `scope: container`, which makes the relation container-scoped.
note: encodeJujuInfoRelation adds the provider with Scope: charm.ScopeGlobal (domain/application/state/state.go:369 adds it when absent). The relation becomes container-scoped if either endpoint is container-scoped (domain/relation/state/relation.go:286). Non-subordinate consumers with a global-scoped requirer are not rejected. Subordinate use is the common convention, not a constraint.

propositions: A secret backend is where Juju stores secret content.
note: The backend types are controller (named 'internal'), kubernetes and vault (internal/secrets/provider/{juju,kubernetes,vault}). 'Service' fits vault and Kubernetes. The default 'internal' backend is the controller's own database, not a separate service, so a precise definition could say 'store (the controller database or an external service)'.

propositions: A subordinate charm's units are placed on the same machine as the principal unit they accompany.
note: A subordinate unit is created when a principal unit enters a container-scoped relation (relation.go:1850-1853) and gets the principal unit's net node (subordinateunit.go:67-83). Strictly, subordinate status is defined by `subordinate: true` in metadata, and co-location is its consequence.
